query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Minor addition of a ductile segregant element (e.g., ~5 at.% Ti) to the equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room‐temperature ductility via grain boundary segregation, without compromising its high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic (equiatomic) single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small amount (~5 at.%) of Ti into the NbMoTaW alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Alloy production and processing under conditions similar to the baseline material; subsequent testing at room temperature, 1600 °C, and under irradiation conditions. The Ti content is kept low to avoid inducing multiphase formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Ti is expected to preferentially segregate to grain boundaries, reducing grain-boundary embrittlement and facilitating dislocation motion across interfaces at room temperature.
generation.mechanism: Grain boundary segregation of Ti lowers the boundary energy and enhances cohesion by promoting more uniform plastic deformation. At high temperatures, the increased diffusion and possible dissolving of Ti maintains the homogeneous BCC matrix, preserving mechanical strength and irradiation resistance predicted by first-principles calculations for the baseline alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, the Ti-doped alloy will exhibit increased ductility (higher strain-to-failure and lower yield stress relative to brittle baseline behavior) without a significant reduction in high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy with excellent performance at 1600 °C and under irradiation but poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the Ti addition is limited (around 5 at.%), ensuring that the alloy remains single-phase BCC; higher Ti levels risk forming secondary phases that could compromise high-temperature performance or irradiation stability.
generation.uncertainty: The precise level of Ti required for optimal grain-boundary modification, and its long-term thermal stability under high-temperature and irradiation conditions, remain to be experimentally confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the NbMoTaW alloy: one as the baseline and one with ~5 at.% Ti addition. Characterize both alloys using microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/SEM with EDS for grain boundary segregation), and then perform standardized tensile tests at room temperature and at 1600 °C. Additionally, subject samples to controlled irradiation (e.g., ion irradiation) and evaluate microstructural changes and mechanical properties post-irradiation.
measurements: Irradiation-induced defect density and mechanical property degradation
Microstructural analysis for phase stability and grain boundary segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared with the baseline, or if high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance is degraded beyond acceptable limits, then the hypothesis is falsified.
